chapters.title: Birth Customs: From the Womb to the Weaning Feast
chapters.subtitle: How Israel welcomed a child, step by step, in the first three years
chapters.nutshell: In the Bible a child is a gift from God, and the first years of life were marked by a clear series of steps: the birth, circumcision and naming on the eighth day, redeeming the firstborn, the mother's purification, and the weaning feast. Luke 2 shows Mary and Joseph walking through these steps with Jesus.
chapters.bigIdea: Every stage of a Jewish child's beginning placed that child, and the family, before God.
skeleton: Children are a blessing, and barren mothers pray
Birth: midwives, washing, salt and swaddling cloths
Day 30 to 40/80: firstborn redeemed, mother purified
About age 2–3: weaning feast and blessing

p: "Children are a heritage from the LORD" (Ps 127:3–5). The first command to humans was "be fruitful and multiply" (Gen 1:28), so a child was a blessing and a sign of hope for the family's future.

That is why barrenness was a deep sorrow. Again and again the Bible tells of mothers who waited and prayed: Sarah, Rebekah (Gen 25:21), Rachel (Gen 30:1, 22), Hannah (1 Sam 1) and Elizabeth (Luke 1). In each story God hears, and the child who is born plays a part in His plan.

Women helped women. Midwives appear in Genesis (35:17; 38:28), and the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah "feared God" and refused Pharaoh's order to kill the boys (Ex 1:15–21). Pharaoh told them to watch "on the *ovnayim*" (Ex 1:16), a rare word meaning "two stones". Many understand it as a birthstool, but its meaning is not certain.

Ezekiel 16:4 describes what a newborn normally received: the cord was cut, the baby was washed, rubbed with salt and wrapped in cloths. So when Mary "wrapped him in swaddling cloths" (Luke 2:7, 12), she did what a caring mother did. The sign for the shepherds was not the cloths but the manger.

God told Abraham that every boy was to be circumcised on the eighth day as the sign of the covenant (Gen 17:10–12; Lev 12:3). It mattered so much that it was done even on the Sabbath, a point Jesus Himself used in argument (John 7:22–23).

By New Testament times the boy was named at his circumcision: John (Luke 1:59–63) and Jesus (Luke 2:21). Later Jewish custom added further details, such as an empty "chair of Elijah" and a *sandek*, a man who holds the baby, like a godfather. These are later customs, not described in the Bible.

After giving birth, a mother was in a state of ritual impurity for a set time: 40 days for a boy, 80 for a girl (Lev 12:1–5). This is usually explained as being about the sacred power of blood and life, not about sin or shame. At the end she brought a lamb and a bird; a poor mother could bring two birds (Lev 12:6–8).

Every firstborn son belonged to the LORD, remembering how God spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt (Ex 13:2, 13–15). From one month old he was redeemed for five shekels of silver (Num 18:15–16). The later *pidyon ha-ben* ceremony with a priest on the 31st day is the rabbinic form of this law.

Luke tells how Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to Jerusalem "when the time of their purification was completed" and offered "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons" (Luke 2:22–24) — the offering of a poor family.

There the old man Simeon took the baby in his arms and blessed God: "my eyes have seen your salvation" (Luke 2:25–35). The prophetess Anna, a widow of great age, gave thanks and spoke of the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:36–38).

Mothers usually nursed their children for about two to three years (2 Macc 7:27 mentions three years). Weaning was a happy milestone: "Abraham made a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned" (Gen 21:8). Hannah waited until Samuel was weaned before bringing him to serve at Shiloh (1 Sam 1:22–24).

Parents and grandparents laid hands on children to bless them, as Jacob did for Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen 48:14), and Jesus took children in His arms and blessed them (Mark 10:13–16). Later customs — the Friday-night "Shalom Zachar" gathering for a newborn boy, or naming a baby girl in the synagogue at the Torah reading — come from later Jewish practice.

diagrams.title: Six birth stories in the Bible
diagrams.note: Turn each card to see how the birth fits God's plan.

cards.back: Sarah laughed when she heard the promise. God kept His word, and Abraham named the boy Isaac, "he laughs". Abraham circumcised him on the eighth day and held a feast when he was weaned.
cards.echo: Paul calls Isaac the child of promise (Gal 4:23, 28)

cards.front: Saved by brave midwives and a basket
cards.back: The midwives would not kill Hebrew boys. Moses' mother hid him for three months, then placed him in a basket on the Nile. Pharaoh's daughter adopted him, and his own mother nursed him.
cards.echo: Jesus too escaped a king who killed baby boys (Matt 2:13–18)

cards.front: The answer to a mother's tears
cards.back: Hannah prayed silently at Shiloh and vowed to give her son to the LORD. After he was weaned she brought him to the house of the LORD, and she sang a song of praise.

cards.front: A priest who could not speak
cards.back: Elizabeth was barren and old. The angel told Zechariah in the Temple that she would have a son. At the circumcision Zechariah wrote "His name is John", and his voice returned.
cards.echo: John prepares the way for Jesus (Luke 3:4)

cards.back: Born in Bethlehem and laid in a manger, Jesus was circumcised and named on the eighth day, and later presented in the Temple, where Simeon and Anna recognised Him.
cards.echo: "Born of a woman, born under the law" (Gal 4:4)

cards.front: "Who sinned, this man or his parents?"
cards.back: Some people thought a birth defect must be a punishment for sin. Jesus rejected this: neither he nor his parents sinned; the works of God would be shown in him. Then He healed him.
cards.echo: Jesus is "the light of the world" (John 9:5)

diagrams.title: From birth to weaning
diagrams.note: The steps the Law set for a newborn and its mother.

events.d: Cord cut, baby washed, rubbed with salt and swaddled (Ezek 16:4; Luke 2:7).
The mother is ritually unclean for 7 days for a boy, 14 for a girl (Lev 12:2, 5).
The boy receives the covenant sign and, by NT times, his name (Gen 17:12; Lev 12:3; Luke 1:59; 2:21).
From one month old, a firstborn son is redeemed for five shekels (Num 18:15–16).
She brings a lamb and a bird, or two birds if poor (Lev 12:4–8; Luke 2:22–24).
A family celebration when the child stops nursing (Gen 21:8; 1 Sam 1:22–24; 2 Macc 7:27).

diagrams.title: The eighth day: circumcision step by step
diagrams.note: Biblical steps first; the last step shows customs that are later.

steps.d: Counted from the birth; not delayed even for the Sabbath (Gen 17:12; John 7:22–23).
Neighbours and relatives come to rejoice with the parents (Luke 1:58–59).
Originally done by the father (Gen 21:4); the sign of the covenant in the flesh (Gen 17:11, 13).
"His name is John"; "he was called Jesus" (Luke 1:63; 2:21).
A trained circumciser (*mohel*), Elijah's chair, the *sandek* and set blessings — later Jewish customs.

cells: Normal loving care for a newborn
Sign of belonging to God's covenant
The name tells the child's story
Return to Temple worship after birth
Two birds when a lamb is too costly
Joy that the child has survived infancy
No NT scene; Samuel's story echoed in Luke 1–2
Laying hands to pass on blessing

diagrams.title: Luke 2: the Law and what Mary and Joseph did
diagrams.note: Luke stresses five times that they did everything "according to the Law" (Luke 2:22, 23, 24, 27, 39).

left.label: What the Law required
items: Circumcise a boy on the eighth day (Lev 12:3)
The mother is purified after 40 days for a boy (Lev 12:2–4)
Offer a lamb and a bird; the poor may offer two birds (Lev 12:6–8)
Every firstborn son belongs to the LORD and is redeemed (Ex 13:2, 13; Num 18:15–16)
No rule that the baby must be brought to the Temple

right.label: What Mary and Joseph did
items: Jesus was circumcised and named on the eighth day (Luke 2:21)
They came "when the days of their purification were completed" (Luke 2:22)
They offered "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons" — a poor family (Luke 2:24)
They presented Jesus to the Lord; Luke mentions no payment (Luke 2:22–23)
They brought Jesus Himself, where Simeon and Anna met Him (Luke 2:25–38)

verses.text: Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward.
If she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons.
At the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus.
For my eyes have seen your salvation.
Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.

keyPoints: In the Bible children are a heritage and blessing from the LORD, and barren mothers' prayers are answered in key stories.
A newborn was washed, rubbed with salt and swaddled; Mary's swaddling cloths were ordinary motherly care.
Boys were circumcised on the eighth day, even on the Sabbath, and by NT times were named that day.
The mother's purification (40/80 days) ended with an offering; Mary and Joseph brought the poor family's two birds.
The firstborn son was redeemed for five shekels; children were nursed for about 2–3 years and weaning was celebrated.
reflect: Mary and Joseph kept the Law carefully even though they were poor. What does that tell you about the home Jesus grew up in?
Simeon and Anna waited many years to see God's promise. What are you waiting for in faith?

quiz.q: On which day was a Jewish boy circumcised?
quiz.why: Gen 17:12 and Lev 12:3 set the eighth day; it was done even on the Sabbath (John 7:22–23).

quiz.q: What did Mary and Joseph's offering of two birds show?
quiz.why: Lev 12:8 allows two birds when the family cannot afford a lamb (Luke 2:24).

quiz.q: How much was paid to redeem a firstborn son?
quiz.why: Num 18:15–16: from one month old, five shekels by the sanctuary shekel.

quiz.q: Which of these is a later Jewish custom, not described in the Bible?
options: Naming a boy at his circumcision
quiz.why: The weaning feast (Gen 21:8), swaddling (Ezek 16:4) and naming at circumcision (Luke 1:59) are biblical; Elijah's chair is later.

terms.def: "Covenant of circumcision" — the eighth-day circumcision of a Jewish boy (Gen 17).
"Two stones" (Ex 1:16); probably a birthstool, though the meaning is uncertain.
The mother's return to ritual purity after 40 or 80 days, ended by an offering (Lev 12).
"Redemption of the son": buying back the firstborn for five shekels (Num 18:16); the ceremony form is later.
A celebration when a child stopped nursing, at about 2–3 years (Gen 21:8).
In later Jewish custom, the honoured man who holds the baby during circumcision.

chapters.title: Naming Customs: What's in a Hebrew Name
chapters.subtitle: Names that tell a story, carry God's name, or announce a calling
chapters.nutshell: In the Bible a name (*shem*) is more than a label: it often tells the story of a birth, carries God's name, or announces a calling. Mothers, fathers and sometimes God Himself gave names, and God gave new names when He gave new tasks.
chapters.bigIdea: A Hebrew name was a short sentence about who a person was and what God was doing.
skeleton: A name is identity and calling
Who named the child: mother, father or God
Names from circumstances and names with God's name
"Son of" names, nicknames and double names
A new name in the age to come

p: The Hebrew word *shem* means "name", but also reputation and character. "A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches" (Prov 22:1). To "call on the name of the LORD" is to call on God Himself.
So parents did not choose names only for their sound. A name could remember a prayer, a sorrow, a joy or a promise, and people expected it to say something true about the child.

Mothers very often named their children: Leah and Rachel named Jacob's sons (Gen 29–30), and Hannah named Samuel (1 Sam 1:20). Fathers named too: Lamech named Noah (Gen 5:29), and Jacob renamed his dying wife's "Ben-oni" ("son of my sorrow") as "Benjamin" ("son of the right hand", Gen 35:18).

Sometimes God chose the name before birth: Ishmael (Gen 16:11), Isaac (Gen 17:19), John (Luke 1:13) and Jesus (Matt 1:21). Through Nathan God also gave Solomon the name Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD" (2 Sam 12:25).

Many names are wordplays on what happened at the birth. Jacob's twelve sons each carry a short story (Gen 29:32–30:24; 35:18). Moses means "drawn out" because he was drawn out of the water (Ex 2:10). Ichabod, "no glory", was named when the ark was captured (1 Sam 4:21).

Other names carry God's name. Names with *-el* contain "God": Daniel ("God is my judge"), Michael ("who is like God?"). Names with *-yah* or *Yeho-* contain the LORD's name: Isaiah ("the LORD saves"), Elijah ("my God is the LORD"), Jehoshaphat ("the LORD judges") and *Yeshua*, Jesus ("the LORD saves").

When God gave someone a new role, He sometimes gave a new name: Abram became Abraham, "father of many nations" (Gen 17:5); Sarai became Sarah (Gen 17:15); Jacob became Israel (Gen 32:28); Moses renamed Hoshea as Joshua (Num 13:16).

Jesus named Simon "Cephas", Aramaic for "rock" — Peter in Greek (John 1:42; Matt 16:18). Saul is also called Paul from Acts 13:9; this was probably his Roman name used among Gentiles rather than a name given at his conversion.

sections.h: Naming at the circumcision and family names
p: When John was circumcised, the relatives wanted to call him Zechariah after his father, but Elizabeth said "He shall be called John", and Zechariah wrote "His name is John" (Luke 1:59–63). Their surprise — "none of your relatives is called by this name" (1:61) — suggests that naming after a relative was common, though not a fixed rule.

People were also known as "son of" — Hebrew *ben*, Aramaic *bar*: Simon Bar-Jonah (Matt 16:17), Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46), Barabbas ("son of the father"), Barnabas, "son of encouragement" (Acts 4:36). There were nicknames too: James and John were "Boanerges, sons of thunder" (Mark 3:17).

sections.h: Two languages, later customs, a new name
p: In a world of Aramaic and Greek, many had a name in each: Tabitha (Aramaic) and Dorcas (Greek) both mean "gazelle" (Acts 9:36); Thomas and Didymus both mean "twin" (John 11:16); John was also called Mark (Acts 12:12).

Later Jewish customs differ: Ashkenazi Jews usually name a child after a relative who has died, while Sephardi Jews often name after living grandparents — these are later practices. And God promises the faithful "a new name" written on a white stone (Rev 2:17; compare Isa 62:2).

diagrams.title: Kinds of names in the Bible
Jacob's sons and the stories in their names
diagrams.note: The meanings are wordplays on similar-sounding Hebrew words.

cells: "See, a son!" — the LORD has seen my misery
"Heard" — the LORD heard I was unloved
"Attached" — now my husband will be attached
"Praise" — this time I will praise the LORD
"My wrestling" — I have wrestled with my sister
"Reward / hire" — God has given me my wages
"Honour / dwell" — my husband will honour me
"May he add" — another son; God took away my reproach
"Son of my sorrow" renamed "son of the right hand"

diagrams.title: Eight name changes
diagrams.note: A new name usually marks a new calling or a new chapter of life.

cards.back: God renamed Abram when He made the covenant of circumcision: "your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations."
cards.echo: Abraham is father of all who believe (Rom 4:16–17)

cards.front: A princess and mother of nations
cards.back: Both forms mean "princess". The new name came with the promise that she would bear a son and be the mother of nations and kings.
cards.echo: Sarah is honoured for her faith (Heb 11:11)

cards.front: The one who wrestled with God
cards.back: After wrestling through the night at the Jabbok, Jacob was told: "Your name shall no longer be Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed."
cards.echo: The whole people is called Israel after him

cards.front: From sorrow to the right hand
cards.back: Rachel, dying in childbirth, named her son "son of my sorrow". Jacob renamed him "son of the right hand", a name of strength and favour.
cards.echo: Paul was proud to be of the tribe of Benjamin (Phil 3:5)

cards.back: Before sending the spies, Moses renamed Hoshea son of Nun as Joshua (Yehoshua), adding the LORD's name to his name.
cards.echo: Yeshua, Jesus, is a short form of the same name (Matt 1:21)

cards.front: A second name sent by a prophet
cards.back: When Solomon was born, the LORD loved him and sent Nathan to name him Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD". He is still known as Solomon.
Jesus looked at Simon and said, "You shall be called Cephas" — Aramaic for rock, Petros in Greek. Later He said He would build His church on this rock.

cards.front: Not a conversion name, but a second name
cards.back: Luke simply says "Saul, who was also called Paul". He likely had both names from birth — a Hebrew name and a Roman one — and used Paul in his mission to the Gentiles.
cards.echo: He still calls himself a Hebrew of Hebrews (Phil 3:5)

diagrams.title: Luke 1:63: "His name is John"
diagrams.note: The Greek name Iōannēs comes from Hebrew Yochanan, "the LORD has been gracious" — fitting for a son given to an old, barren couple.

readings.label: Word for word
readings.text: Having asked for a tablet, he wrote, saying: **John** is his name.

readings.label: Common English (ESV)
readings.text: And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, "His name is John."
readings.note: Zechariah could not speak, so he wrote.

readings.label: Behind the name (Hebrew)
readings.text: יוֹחָנָן Yochanan = Yo- (the LORD) + chanan (has been gracious)
readings.note: The angel had already given this name (Luke 1:13).

diagrams.title: How a child received a name

steps.d: The mother's or father's first words often became the name (Gen 29:32; 35:18).
The name remembers an answered prayer, a joy or a sorrow (1 Sam 1:20; 1 Sam 4:21).
A name given before birth (Gen 17:19; Luke 1:13; Matt 1:21).
By NT times the name was given at the circumcision (Luke 1:59–63; 2:21).
John showed God's grace; Jesus saves His people from their sins (Matt 1:21).

verses.text: A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches.
You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.
And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, "His name is John."
Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel.
I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone.

keyPoints: A Hebrew name (*shem*) speaks of identity, character and calling, not only a label.
Mothers often named children, fathers also did, and sometimes God gave the name before birth.
Many names tell the story of a birth (Jacob's sons, Moses, Ichabod) or carry God's name (-el, -yah, Yeho-).
God gave new names with new callings: Abraham, Sarah, Israel, Joshua, Peter.
By NT times a boy was named at his circumcision; "son of" names, nicknames and Aramaic–Greek double names were common.
reflect: Jesus' name means "the LORD saves". How has that name been true in your own life?
God promises a new name to those who overcome (Rev 2:17). What does it mean to you that God knows you by name?

quiz.q: Who named most of Jacob's sons in Genesis 29–30?
quiz.why: Leah and Rachel named the sons, including the sons of their servants Bilhah and Zilpah.

quiz.q: What does the name Yeshua (Jesus) mean?
quiz.why: Yeshua is a short form of Yehoshua, "the LORD saves" (Matt 1:21).

quiz.q: Why were the relatives surprised at the name John (Luke 1:61)?
options: It was given before the eighth day
quiz.why: "None of your relatives is called by this name" — naming after a relative seems to have been common.

quiz.q: Which of these is a nickname Jesus gave?
quiz.why: Jesus called James and John Boanerges (Mark 3:17). Barnabas was a name given by the apostles (Acts 4:36).

terms.def: Hebrew for "name" — also reputation, character and presence.
A name that contains God's name, such as -el (God) or -yah / Yeho- (the LORD).
"Son of" in Hebrew (ben) and Aramaic (bar), as in Bar-Jonah or Bartimaeus.
Hebrew form of John: "the LORD has been gracious".
Hebrew/Aramaic name of Jesus, short for Yehoshua (Joshua): "the LORD saves".
